lesson.title: Same Shape, Same Size: Triangles and the Rules of Congruence
lesson.summary: Triangle congruence criteria let you prove two triangles match exactly in every side and angle using only a few pieces of information, and they must not be confused with the separate, weaker idea of similarity.
lesson.body:
The interior angles of any triangle always add up to 180 degrees. One way to see why traces directly back to the previous chapter: draw a line through one vertex of the triangle that runs parallel to the opposite side. The angles formed along that new line, together with the triangle's own angles, form alternate interior angle pairs with the transversal lines are the triangle's other two sides, and those alternate interior angles are equal to the triangle's base angles. Laid along the straight line, the three angles from the triangle line up to form a straight angle, which measures 180 degrees, confirming the angle sum. A related fact, the exterior angle theorem, states that an exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two remote interior angles, the two angles not adjacent to it.

Two triangles are congruent if they are identical in every measurement, every pair of corresponding sides equal in length and every pair of corresponding angles equal in measure, meaning one triangle could be picked up and placed exactly on top of the other. This is a stronger claim than similarity, where two triangles have the same shape and equal corresponding angles but their sides are only required to be proportional, not equal, so similar triangles can be different sizes while congruent triangles cannot.

Proving two triangles congruent does not require checking all six corresponding parts, three sides and three angles, individually. A short list of criteria guarantees full congruence from partial information: SSS, all three pairs of corresponding sides equal, SAS, two pairs of corresponding sides equal along with the included angle between them, ASA, two pairs of corresponding angles equal along with the included side between them, AAS, two pairs of corresponding angles equal along with a non-included side, and HL, used only for right triangles, where the hypotenuse and one leg are equal. It is essential not to confuse these with the similarity criteria AA, SAS similarity, and SSS similarity, which only establish proportional sides and equal angles, not the full equality that congruence requires. A criterion like SSA, where the two known sides do not include the given angle, is notably not on this list, because that combination does not guarantee a unique triangle.

Find the missing angle in a triangle with two known angles of 50 degrees and 60 degrees. Since the three interior angles must sum to 180 degrees, the third angle is 180 - 50 - 60, which is 70 degrees.

Now consider two right triangles, each with a hypotenuse of length 13 and one leg of length 5. By the Pythagorean theorem, the remaining leg in each triangle satisfies leg^2 + 5^2 = 13^2, so leg^2 = 13^2 - 5^2, which is 169 - 25, equal to 144, and the square root of 144 is 12. So each triangle has legs 5 and 12 with hypotenuse 13, the well known 5-12-13 right triangle. Because both right triangles share an equal hypotenuse of 13 and an equal corresponding leg of 5, the HL criterion guarantees the two triangles are congruent, and indeed the computation confirms the second leg matches too, 12 in both cases, exactly as HL promises it must.

On the ACT, the fastest way to avoid mixing up congruence and similarity is to ask whether the problem gives you enough matching information to force an exact copy, congruence, or only enough to force the same shape at a possibly different scale, similarity, and then to reach for the matching criterion, SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, or HL for congruence, rather than assuming any set of three matching parts is automatically enough.
